attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own newsletter, stated as his estimate.

semantics.note: Keeps the OpenAI exclusion, the under-$3B-per-quarter threshold, the 'revenue, not profit' point and the ~$293B four-year spend. It is a present-tense observation built on his own estimate.

contract.note: Using realized revenue for the latest quarter (Jan–Mar 2026) is a fair plain reading. Requiring AI-only capex may be stricter than his wording, which just says 'spent'. That doesn't decide the result here, because the revenue part can't be resolved either.

evidence.note: A Microsoft disclosure of a $37B annual run rate for its whole AI business. It is annualized, includes OpenAI, and gives no customer breakdown, so it can't test realized quarterly revenue excluding OpenAI.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only Microsoft's total AI run rate. It has no realized quarterly AI revenue, no figure for OpenAI's contribution, and no reconciliation of the ~$293B spending. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition can be checked.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, which he re-quotes from his own earlier newsletter and endorses.

semantics.note: Naming the two companies as OpenAI and Anthropic is justified by the context. The proposition keeps all four parts: majority revenue share, losses in the billions, no path to profitability, and payments that depend on funding.

contract.note: The compound claim gets a reasonable plain reading: more than 50% of realized AI revenue, a profitability path judged on economics at the time, and a cash-shortfall test for funding dependence. 'No path to profitability' leans rhetorical, but the contract's reading of it is fair.

evidence.note: Microsoft's annualized AI run rate. It doesn't give the labs' share and isn't realized quarterly revenue.
AWS segment sales include non-AI services and have no customer breakdown, so they aren't the right denominator.
Shows Amazon's staged investment in OpenAI. It doesn't show that OpenAI's current payments depend on that money.

The S-1, filed before the cutoff, shows large Anthropic net losses in the billions even excluding fair-value charges. It partly backs the losses part for Anthropic only. Its risk language doesn't show there was no path to profitability.

reviews.rationale: No customer share of realized hyperscaler AI revenue is established for Q1 2026, so the main 'most AI revenues' part can't be tested. Anthropic's losses are documented, but there is no data on OpenAI and no cash-shortfall test. The funding-dependence and profitability-path parts remain unsettled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own description of the deal structure in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Keeps the core sequence: Anthropic buys TPUs from Google, then rents the same TPUs from Google. The Broadcom development step is left out, but that doesn't change what has to be tested.

contract.note: The literal reading of separate buy and rent-back steps matches his explicit wording. Limiting the test to terms agreed by the post date is fair.

evidence.note: Anthropic's S-1, filed before the cutoff, shows Broadcom master equipment leases to Anthropic's special-purpose subsidiaries, with hardware in facilities run by others on its behalf. Anthropic pays rent to Broadcom, not Google.

Reporting on the lease exhibit (effective March 31, 2026) says Google sells the TPUs to Broadcom and Broadcom leases them to Anthropic's subsidiary. Google and its affiliates are excluded as data-centre operators.
Google's April 2026 announcement describes two channels: Google Cloud services and TPUs supplied through Broadcom. It does not describe a purchase followed by renting back from Google.

reviews.rationale: The agreement in place before the post, dated March 31, 2026, has a different chain: Google sells to Broadcom, Broadcom leases to an Anthropic subsidiary, and the hardware is hosted by operators other than Google. Anthropic neither buys the TPUs from Google nor rents them back from Google. This meets the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'making it up' accusation, the single-interview basis and the stylized-facts caveat. It is an observation about what public evidence existed.

contract.note: Reading 'making it up' as 'no other evidentiary basis existed' is a fair, ordinary reading. It doesn't require proving anyone's intent. Reading 'profitable on inference' as a positive margin after inference costs is reasonable.

evidence.note: The transcript shows Amodei setting Anthropic aside and calling his numbers stylized. That supports the caveat part. Calling it a company disclosure is a loose label, but the item is genuine.
Epoch's analysis from Feb 2026, before the post, cites reporting of a 40% Anthropic gross margin. That is a separate, company-specific public basis for positive inference margins.

reviews.rationale: The caveat part holds: Amodei did disclaim the numbers as Anthropic's. But reporting before the post already gave a company-specific basis for positive inference margins. So the central claim, that such statements rest only on that interview and are made up, fails the contract's contradiction condition.
